findings.evidence: Wrenford "tepa" = wood: coined for "planks" by Dace·6 (generation 6) · Oakhollow "tepa" = wood: coined for "planks" by Dace·6 (generation 6) · Oakhollow "beka" = three: misheard: peka → beka (generation 25)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.71, p = 0.016, n = 12. Most used: two (5% replaced per generation), wood (9% replaced per generation), food (4% replaced per generation); least: planks (34%), five (52%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 15, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.14, p = 0.500, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
